Prospero tells Miranda that if she remembers anything from before she came to the island, she may also remember how she came there. In other words, her memory of the women who tended her suggests she might recall her arrival too. Choice A fails because Prospero confirms the memory is real ("Thou hadst, and more"), not a daydream.

fix.passage:
The following text is from William Shakespeare's play The Tempest, first performed in 1611. Miranda has lived on an island with her father, Prospero, since she was three years old. Prospero has stated that Miranda likely does not remember anything other than her life on the island.

MIRANDA: 'Tis far off, And rather like a dream than an assurance That my remembrance warrants. Had I not Four or five women once that tended me?

PROSPERO: Thou hadst, and more, Miranda. But how is it That this lives in thy mind? What seest thou else In the dark backward and abysm of time? If thou remember'st ought ere thou camest here, How thou camest here thou mayst.

"Lawmakers" is a plain plural subject (the people who did the designating), so it needs no apostrophe. The fossil belongs to the state, so the possessive "state's" is required. The other choices either put an apostrophe on "lawmakers" or leave "states" without the possessive apostrophe.
Both "works" and "writers" are simple plurals here; nothing belongs to them, so neither takes an apostrophe. The choices with "work's" or "writer's" wrongly turn plural nouns into possessives.

"Called the chromophore" is one tight phrase: the verb "is called" is directly followed by the name. Any punctuation between "called" and "the chromophore" would split the verb from its complement, so no punctuation is correct.

The phrase "cores now number in the dozens, hundreds, or even thousands" is an interruption that opens with a dash, so it must close with a matching dash. The sentence then continues "so drastically ... that the once-revolutionary dual-core technology ... can be found," which needs "that" right after the closing dash. Choice C breaks the "so ... that" structure with a period, and D mixes a dash with a comma.

The pronoun refers back to "a given industry," which is singular, so "it" and the singular verb "consists" fit. "They" and "these" are plural, and "this" is vague about what it refers to.

The narrator first makes a general claim: on a boat, each crew member thinks he is doing all the work. He then supports it with the specific views of Harris and George on this trip. Choice A fails because the narrator says he has "always noticed" this, so it isn't unexpected.

fix.passage:
The following text is from Jerome K. Jerome's 1889 novel Three Men in a Boat (To Say Nothing of the Dog). The narrator and two friends are taking a boat down the River Thames in England.

In a boat, I have always noticed that it is the fixed idea of each member of the crew that he is doing everything. Harris's notion was, that it was he alone who had been working, and that both George and I had been imposing upon him. George, on the other hand, ridiculed the idea of Harris's having done anything more than eat and sleep, and had a cast-iron opinion that it was he—George himself—who had done all the labour worth speaking of.

explanation: Lorde argues poets can write between shifts, so earning a living another way doesn't stop them. Text 2 says serious poetry takes time that people with full-time jobs often lack, so financial security shapes who becomes a poet. They would disagree on whether a full-time job is a major obstacle to poetry. Choice A is something both would likely agree on, since neither denies that other arts need time and money.

fix.passage:
Text 1
The poet Audre Lorde once claimed that poetry is the most inexpensive of art forms to practice. While people who pursue other art forms—painting, architecture, theater—require large blocks of uninterrupted time as well as money to complete their work, poets can write, as Lorde said, "between shifts, in the hospital pantry, on the subway, and on scraps of surplus paper." So poets can practice their art even if they must earn their living in another way.

Text 2
Any assessment of the state of contemporary poetry must reckon with the professionalization of the field. While it is possible in theory for anyone to publish in Virginia Quarterly Review, Kenyon Review, or a similar major poetry outlet, many people who do so have professional training in poetry and extensive practice writing it, which requires time not often available to those who must also work full-time jobs. Thus, financial security indirectly affects which people become poets.

With large vortices, intermediate-headed fish feel strong pressure at the snout while wide-headed fish feel little, so the hypothesis predicts intermediate-headed fish should avoid obstacles better. If the intermediate-headed dusky smooth-hound bumped into obstacles just as often as the wide-headed fish, that prediction fails. Choice C actually supports the hypothesis, since the low-pressure wide-headed fish did worse.

fix.passage: Water flowing around an obstruction creates vortices (swirls) that vary in size with the obstruction's size and position, and fish sense these vortices in order to navigate around the obstructions. Using models of three fish-head shapes—narrow (low ratio of width to length), intermediate, and wide (high ratio of width to length)—Yuzo R. Yanagisuru, Otar Akanyeti, and James C. Liao showed that as vortex size increases, pressure fluctuations at the snout increase for narrow-headed and intermediate-headed fish but remain low for wide-headed fish. A second research team has therefore hypothesized that in low visibility, a fish will be more likely to avoid an obstruction when the associated pressure fluctuations at the fish's snout are greater.

So DptB, not DptA, protects against this bacterium, and since P. rettgeri resistance depends on DptA instead, DptB may have evolved as a specific defense against A. sicearae. Choice A reverses the roles, and D fails because flies with only DptB survive just as well.

fix.passage: In a study of the evolution of DptA and DptB—Diptericin genes encoding antimicrobial peptides that combat pathogens and foster beneficial microbes in fruit flies (Drosophila)—researchers assessed Drosophila melanogaster resistance to pathogenic infections by Providencia rettgeri and Acetobacter sicearae, bacteria common in the flies' environments. Subjects included flies identified by mutations silencing DptA, DptB, or both DptA and DptB (termed types A, B, and AB, respectively). explanation: Older dogs have had more exposure to language. If the gap between their brain responses to the familiar and unfamiliar language is greatest in older dogs, then more exposure goes with better distinguishing familiar from unfamiliar languages. Choice A shows dogs can tell the languages apart but no link to amount of exposure, and D compares speech to scrambled noise rather than two languages.

fix.passage: Neurobiologists Laura Cuaya, Raúl Hernández-Pérez, and colleagues investigated the language detection abilities of eighteen dogs raised in similar settings. The researchers monitored the brain activity of Barney (a golden retriever), Mini (a mixed breed), and other dogs while the animals listened to three recordings: one of The Little Prince being read in Spanish, the second in Hungarian, and a third made up of short, randomly selected fragments of the first two, scrambled so that they didn't resemble human speech. Each dog was familiar with either Spanish or Hungarian, but not both. The team concluded that the amount of previous language exposure a dog has received may influence its ability to distinguish familiar languages from unfamiliar ones.

In a study of zoo chimpanzees in Norway and other mid-latitude countries, Sophie Moittié and colleagues found not only that chimpanzees' vitamin D levels correlate with UVB irradiance but also that vitamin D levels show no evidence of plateauing as UVB irradiance reaches its highest local levels, suggesting that _____.

explanation: The first clause says divergent strategies emerged, and the clause after the blank explains what those strategies were. A colon correctly joins an independent clause to one that explains it. A comma alone (C) would create a comma splice, and no punctuation (B) or "and" (A) runs the clauses together incorrectly.

"Novelist" is a title placed directly before the name, so "novelist Stephen Graham Jones" works as one unit with no commas. Also, the phrase "to craft the entry" belongs to the verb, so no comma should separate it from the name.

The subject is "accomplishments," which is plural, so the verb must be plural: "attest." The phrase "of Goldin, winner of the 2023 Nobel Prize..." sits between subject and verb and can make the singular forms ("attests," "has attested," "is attesting") seem right.

After the comma, "its vehicles highly prized by collectors..." is an absolute phrase that adds detail to the main clause, so it needs a participle, not a full verb. Choices B, C, and D add a finite verb, which would create a second independent clause joined only by a comma (a comma splice).

"Finland" identifies which fellow OECD member nation is meant, so it is essential information and takes no punctuation: "fellow OECD member nation Finland." Choices A, B, and C set Finland off as if it were extra information, which isn't right in this construction.

The main verb of the sentence is "had ... been essentially gathering dust," so "much admired during his lifetime ... and in the decades that followed" must be a nonessential phrase set off by commas. A comma after "works" opens it, matching the comma after "followed." Choices B, C, and D add another verb ("were," "had been"), giving the subject two main verbs.

The first sentence says the change was driven by demand for "certain grains"; the next sentence names those grains, maize and wheat. "In particular" signals that move from general to specific. "By comparison" and "alternatively" suggest contrasts the text doesn't make.

The sentence says not every element was isolated soon after discovery; for those elements, the isolation process frequently took a few years, as the molybdenum example shows. "Often" correctly describes how commonly this delay happened. "Even so" signals a contrast, and "similarly" would wrongly compare these elements to quickly isolated ones like phosphorus.

The previous sentence explains that the Roman numerals show the order in which moons were named, not their distance from Jupiter. The final sentence draws a conclusion from that: so it's wrong to assume Eirene is the 57th moon from the planet. "Then" (meaning "therefore") signals this conclusion. "However" would signal a contrast, but the last sentence follows from, rather than contradicts, the one before it.
note: PDF says C (however); the last sentence is a conclusion drawn from the previous sentence, so 'then' (D) is the logical transition.
